tagline: A letter of hope from the apostle Peter to scattered believers in Asia Minor who were suffering as outsiders for the name of Christ.
overview:
First Peter is written to Christians who have become strangers in their own towns. Their neighbors find them odd, slander them, and sometimes abuse them, because they no longer join in the festivals, drinking, and religious life that once bound them to everyone else. Peter does not tell them that suffering is unreal or that it will soon go away. He tells them who they are: people born again into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus, chosen by God, a holy nation and a royal priesthood, heirs of an inheritance that cannot spoil. And he tells them how to live: with holiness, with love for one another, with honorable conduct that silences slander, and with the steady trust of those who follow a Savior who suffered before he was glorified.

The letter moves between the great truths of salvation and the ordinary settings where faith is tested: the relationship of citizens to rulers, household servants to masters, wives to unbelieving husbands, husbands to wives, elders to their flocks. Again and again it returns to one pattern, drawn from Christ himself, of suffering now and glory to follow.

First Peter has been loved by persecuted churches in every century because it takes suffering seriously without surrendering to despair. It gives readers a way to understand hostility that neither retaliates nor retreats, and it grounds that way in the cross and resurrection. It also contains one of the New Testament's most puzzling passages, Christ's proclamation to the spirits in prison (3:18-22), which has shaped Christian confession about Christ's descent to the dead.
author:
The letter opens with “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1) and closes with Peter calling himself a fellow elder and “a witness of Christ’s sufferings” (5:1). It says it was written “Through Silvanus” (5:12). Silvanus is almost certainly the Silas of Acts (the Greek and Latin forms of the same name), a leader in the Jerusalem church who later traveled with Paul (Acts 15:22, 40; 1 Thessalonians 1:1). The phrase may mean that Silvanus carried the letter to its readers, or that he served as Peter's secretary and helped shape its Greek, or both. Early Christian writers accepted the letter as Peter's: it appears to be echoed by Polycarp in the early second century, Eusebius reports that Papias used it, and by the late second century Irenaeus cited it by name. Eusebius counted it among the undisputed books.

Many modern scholars regard it as pseudonymous, written by a follower of Peter, perhaps a circle of his disciples in Rome, after his death. They point to its polished Greek and its use of the Greek Old Testament, which they think unlikely from a Galilean fisherman described in Acts 4:13 as unschooled; to its many parallels with Paul's letters; to the absence of personal memories of Jesus; and to what they read as a later situation of persecution. Those who hold to Petrine authorship reply that the help of Silvanus explains the Greek, that Peter had decades of ministry among Greek speakers, that shared early Christian teaching explains the parallels with Paul, and that the suffering described is local social hostility rather than an empire-wide campaign, which fits the 60s as well as any later date.
date: If Peter wrote the letter, it comes before his death, which early tradition places in Rome under the emperor Nero, most likely in the persecution that followed the great fire of AD 64. That points to about AD 62 to 64. The letter's calm counsel to honor the emperor (2:17) may suggest a time before Nero's violence against Christians became open policy, though Peter could have written it in the shadow of that violence. Scholars who regard the letter as pseudonymous usually date it between about AD 70 and 95, and some later, sometimes connecting it with conditions under Domitian or with the situation reflected in the letter of Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia and Pontus, who wrote to the emperor Trajan around AD 110 to 112 asking how to deal with people accused of being Christians.
setting:
The readers live in “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), Roman provinces covering much of Asia Minor, the region of modern Turkey north and west of the Taurus mountains. The order of the names may trace the route of a messenger who landed on the Black Sea coast, circled through the interior, and returned near where he began, though that is a scholarly suggestion rather than something the letter says. These were mostly towns and countryside, not only the great cities, and the churches there are not described in Acts, except for parts of Asia and Galatia.

Peter calls his readers exiles and foreigners, borrowing Israel's language of the Dispersion, but most of them were Gentile converts: they had inherited an empty way of life from their ancestors (1:18) and had once lived in the pagan vices of their neighbors (4:3-4). Conversion cut them off from civic festivals, trade guild banquets, and household worship of the gods, and that withdrawal made them look antisocial and suspicious. The letter reflects slander, insult, and local mistreatment rather than an organized imperial persecution. Peter writes from “Babylon” (5:13), which most interpreters, ancient and modern, take as a code name for Rome, the imperial capital that like ancient Babylon ruled the world and held God's people in exile. Revelation uses the name the same way (Revelation 14:8; 17:5), as did some Jewish writings after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. A few interpreters take it literally, as the Mesopotamian city with its Jewish community, or as a Roman fortress town called Babylon in Egypt, but these views have few defenders.
purpose: Peter writes, in his own summary, to encourage the readers and to testify “that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it” (5:12). He wants suffering believers to understand their identity (chosen, born again, God's own people), to see their suffering in light of Christ's suffering and coming glory, and to live in a way that commends the gospel to outsiders. The letter holds together two concerns that are often separated: faithful endurance under hostility, and respectful, good conduct within the structures of ordinary society. It aims to keep the readers from both despair and retaliation.
story: First Peter belongs to the period after the resurrection and Pentecost, when the gospel had spread well beyond Judea and communities of Gentile believers were learning to live as God's people without a homeland. It reaches back through the whole Old Testament story to describe them. Like Israel in Egypt, they have been redeemed by the blood of a spotless lamb (1:19). Like Israel at Sinai, they are called a royal priesthood and a holy nation (2:9, drawing on Exodus 19:6). Like Israel in Babylon, they are exiles waiting for home. Noah and the flood (3:20), Sarah (3:6), and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 (2:22-25) all appear. The letter looks forward to the revelation of Jesus Christ at the end, the same hope the Bible's final book depicts.
christ: Christ is at the center of every movement in 1 Peter. He is the spotless lamb whose blood redeems (1:18-19), the living stone rejected by men but chosen by God and made the cornerstone (2:4-8), and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 who “bore our sins in His body on the tree” (2:24). He is the example whose steps his people follow, who did not retaliate when he was abused (2:21-23). He “suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God” (3:18), was raised, and now sits at God's right hand with every power subject to him (3:22). He is the Shepherd and Overseer of souls (2:25) and the Chief Shepherd who will appear (5:4). Peter also sees him as the one the prophets searched for, their longing directed by the Spirit of Christ toward his sufferings and the glories to follow (1:10-11).
reading:
Read 1 Peter as a real letter to real people under pressure, full of the language of worship and early Christian teaching. Watch for its repeated pattern of suffering followed by glory, which applies first to Christ and then to those who belong to him. Notice how many Old Testament titles for Israel are given to a largely Gentile church, and ask what that meant for people who had lost their place in their own society.

The household instructions (2:13-3:7) need careful reading. They belong to a form found in ancient moral writing, the household code, which set out duties of wives, children, and slaves. Peter uses the form but addresses slaves and wives as moral agents with their own relationship to God, grounds their conduct in Christ rather than in the master's or husband's authority, and requires husbands to honor their wives as fellow heirs. Christians disagree about how these instructions apply today, especially regarding marriage; the letter itself nowhere endorses abuse, and its concern is faithful witness under unjust treatment, not the silencing of victims. Finally, 3:18-22 and 4:6 are among the hardest passages in the New Testament; the chapter notes set out the main readings.

structure.title: The identity of God's people
structure.summary: After the greeting, Peter praises God for new birth into a living hope, calls the readers to holiness as those redeemed by Christ's blood, and describes them as living stones built into a spiritual house, God's chosen people.

structure.title: Honorable conduct among outsiders
structure.summary: As foreigners and exiles, believers are to live so well that slander fails: submitting to rulers, servants to masters after Christ's example, wives and husbands in mutual honor, and all of them repaying evil with blessing.

structure.title: Suffering for doing good
structure.summary: Peter explains how to suffer for righteousness: with a ready defense of hope, after the pattern of Christ who suffered, died, and was raised. He calls for sober, loving community in the last days and for joy in sharing Christ's sufferings.

structure.title: Elders, humility, and final greetings
structure.summary: Peter exhorts the elders to shepherd willingly, calls all to humility and watchfulness against the devil, promises restoration after suffering, and sends greetings from Babylon.

themes.title: Living hope
themes.body: The letter opens with praise for new birth “into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1:3). Hope in 1 Peter is not wishful thinking but confident expectation grounded in a past event and fixed on a future one, the revelation of Christ. Believers are to set their hope fully on that coming grace, and to be ready to explain the hope within them to anyone who asks.

themes.title: Suffering and glory
themes.body: Peter never treats suffering as an accident or a sign that God has abandoned his people. He calls it a testing that refines faith like gold, a share in the sufferings of Christ, and a brief season before glory. He distinguishes suffering for doing good from suffering earned by wrongdoing, and he tells believers to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator.

themes.title: Exiles and God's people
themes.body: The readers are exiles, foreigners, and resident aliens, and yet they are also God's chosen people, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation. The loss of social belonging is answered by a deeper belonging. Their true home is the inheritance reserved in heaven, and their life on earth is a stay abroad lived in reverent fear.

themes.title: Good conduct as witness
themes.body: Peter repeatedly asks believers to do good, so that those who slander them may be put to shame and may even come to glorify God. This is not a strategy for avoiding trouble but a way of bearing witness under trouble, following Christ who entrusted himself to God rather than retaliating.

themes.title: Holiness
themes.body: Because the God who called them is holy, the readers are to be holy in all their conduct (1:15-16, quoting Leviticus). Holiness here means being set apart for God, which shows itself in turning from former passions, in sincere love for fellow believers, and in sobriety and self-control while waiting for the end.

keyChapters.why: Praise for new birth into a living hope, the call to holiness, and redemption by the precious blood of Christ.
The church as living stones and a royal priesthood, and Christ as the suffering servant whose example his people follow.
The call to be ready with a defense of hope, and the difficult passage on Christ's proclamation to the spirits in prison.
Joy in sharing Christ's sufferings, the only New Testament letter use of the name Christian, and the call to entrust oneself to a faithful Creator.
